Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, I really want to thank you for the opportunity to join you today as we put our heads together to reflect on how to finance development and to do so in a very difficult environment. Under Secretary was clear. The message was clear. The financing of development today is challenged internationally by shifts in donor priorities and is challenged nationally by limited fiscal space and the servicing of debt. As a result, we have large financial gaps that are estimated to be about 4 trillion annually. As a result, we also have a lag in achieving sustainable development goals. So far, only 36% are estimated to be on target. And so if you want to close these gaps, if you want to narrow these gaps, we have to do two things. The first is to mobilize far more resources than we do today. And then the second is to design systems that are going to be effective and make those resources count. The question is, how do we achieve this quantum leap in both the volume and the efficiency of our financing? Now, to answer these questions, I thought we could draw from Archimedes, who said a long time ago, and I would quote, "Give me a lever long enough and a fulcrum on which to place it, and I shall move the world." "Give me a lever and I shall move the world." These words were said over two millennia ago, but I thought I would bring them up because I think they speak to what you are trying to achieve here. Archimedes was trying to lift the world physically, literally. What you're trying to do is to lift the world figuratively to make it a better place. Now, because there's then this similarity in purpose, you are essentially doing the same thing. I thought I would use Archimedes as a background, as a frame of reference to lead our discussion. And if you see Archimedes' bet, He essentially articulates it onto four points. There is first a lever, he's going to talk about a lever, he's going to talk about a goal, which is lift the world, he's going to talk about an anchor point, and the person doing the lifting. In terms of what you are trying to do, we'll also need to talk about four main points. What is the goal that you're trying to achieve? What are the sustainable development goals that are priorities today? What are the entry points? In other words, what are the places, the subpopulations, the policies that are going to make it possible for us to be maximally effective? What is the lever? In other words, what are the financial instruments that we can mobilize? And finally, in terms of agency, what are the people and institutions that are going to lead the charge? And so these are the four points that I'm going to make. I'm going to take you through one of each at a time. and just offer a brief commentary before making one, hopefully, relevant policy suggestion. Let's begin with the goal. Archimedes had one single goal, and it was to lift the world. Unfortunately, you have many, many goals, 17 of them. Now, to make it simple, we can group them in three major boxes. that include the economic box, the social box, and the environmental box. Now, these boxes overlap, that is, they have something in common, but they are also distinct. They are sufficiently distinct that they require individualized attention. Depending on whether now you are most focused on promoting economic growth, making social progress, or focusing on environmental protection, The sources of funding that you can leverage and the rationale for demanding resources are going to be different. The resource, the return on investment that you can expect is also going to be different. For some of the goals or some of the targets, the returns are going to be private and they're going to be public for other resources, or they can be exclusive or non-exclusive. So there's a distinction. to be made and the deliberate attention to be given to each of these goals. It's a mistake to focus on one single goal and assume that the others are going to follow. For instance, many countries today achieve growth but without reduction in poverty, and as a result, you have tremendous growth in inequality. If you really want to reduce inequality, it is important not to assume that you can grow and that growth is going to trickle down. It's important not to assume that you're going to grow and clean later. You have to give dedicated attention to each of these big three pillars. And so that's my first message, right? Match your financing to SDG priority areas and give dedicated attention to each of these pillars. Second point. Given that you have set your priority goals, where do you focus investment? What are the specific policies? What are the specific groups and areas in which you are going to focus your investment for maximum impact and maximum spillover? I'm just going to give you an example of what I mean by maximum impact and spillover. Many countries in the world today have a large so-called youth bulge, that is to say a large population of youth that are unemployed. Now, if you can think about investing strategically in these groups, then you can have a maximum impact because in these countries, this is a large population. That is an age where they make critical decisions about education, about consumption, about migration, and so forth. And therefore, you are going to have an effect that is large and an effect that is immediate. At the same time, you are going to have an effect that can ripple over other groups and benefit other populations. In other words, for instance, it's going to benefit the elderly if you invest in elderly care. It's going to benefit the tutoring industry. It's going to release adults from domestic care. And it can also broaden the tax base. So from investing in one strategic group, in this particular case, youth, you can actually achieve multiple benefits. And so that's what I mean by deep impact. and maximum spillover. And so the second lesson here that I want to focus your attention to is to invest as much as possible in places where the benefits are going to reinforce each other. Third point, which is about the lever, in other words, the financial instruments that you need to mobilize. Archimedes had just one lever. And all he needed from his lever is to be long enough. As long as it's not long enough, it's going to achieve his goal. Unfortunately, we need far more from our levers. We need our levers to be long, to be sturdy, and to be diverse. And so There's a possibility to reach multiple sources and to organize them in a way that is simple. You can think about these sources in terms of domestic versus international, public versus private. And so you have the quadrant that we have here with all of these resources. Now, as you think about these resources, these funding sources in these quadrants, you can quickly see that none is perfect. Each of them has advantages and Each of them has disadvantages and drawbacks. Okay? And so the reason why we need multiple resources is because none is perfect. And by having multiple resources, we are going to have three advantages. The first, of course, is volume. Everything else equal, more funding resources, more funding. The second is complementarity. Some Funding sources are good for some purposes and others would complement elsewhere. So for instance, you can mobilize international funding to promote broad environmental question. You can use local national public funding to support essential services. You can mobilize private resources to fund private consumption. You can mobilize community support to promote and to support those that are left behind. So you have that kind of complementarity going on. At the same time, having a diversity of funding sources builds in some resilience. In case where there'd be one funding source that fails, other can more or less make up for the difference. And so diversification is the name of the game. We have to, as much as possible, complement and boost different funding sources to make them complementary and to make the system complementary and reliable. So that's the third point. The fourth and the final point is about agency and whose responsibility it is to secure the financing. And the simple point here is that financing is more than simply mobilizing resources. It's a long chain of actors and actions that goes from securing the funds and to accounting for these funds. And so along this chain, you have a multiplicity of actors that have to intervene, each of them with a specific role, and they have to work in coordination. Just securing the funds does not guarantee the ultimate result. The enterprise can fall if you have a breakdown at later stage. So we have to think holistically about financing system in ways that include not just the mobilization, but the implementation on the field, the evaluation of the result, and the accounting of the resources that were made available. And so the point here is the need for coordination of multiple actors with a clear definition of responsibilities of each of these set of actors. And so as I close my very brief remarks, I want to return to Archimedes to say that your task is similar, in a sense, to his, but his was far simpler than yours. All he had was one goal. one entry point, one lever, and just one person to run the show. In your case, it's far more complex. You have multiple goals to follow, 17 of them, many, many entry points that are possible and that you need to choose from and coordinate, many financial instruments that you have to combine and match and complement and nurture, and then many institutions that you have to coordinate for maximum efficiency. And so the first challenge before you is one of coordination and efficiency, right? But that's not all. That's probably the least of them. In addition to coordination, there's a challenge of mobilization. Efficiency is not enough. It's clear, as Under Secretary said in his address, that the Sustainable Development Agenda needs more resources And that case has to be made. The case for international cooperation has to be made. And as we make this case, we can use a range of arguments from moral and humanitarian to economic and political to existential argument. The moral argument is to say essentially that the poverty that we see around the world today is the legacy of past exploitation and extraction. And so international cooperation is a form of redress. That is the moral argument. The humanitarian argument is for us to be a great and just society, we are going to be evaluated by how we take care of the least of us. The economic argument is that by lifting those who are left behind, we create markets that are going to benefit everybody. And so it is in our best interest to cooperate. The political argument is that instability anywhere is instability everywhere, instability that can show up at your door. And finally, the existential argument is that we can save this planet. The share of global foreign direct investment flows to SIDS in 2024 remained at less than 1%. Debt service burdens across SIDS have reached two-decade highs. Taken together, these numbers reveal a fundamental problem. We do not face only a shortage of finance. We face a problem of where finance flows, on what terms, and according to whose measure of need. Too often, countries facing the greatest vulnerabilities encounter the highest cost of capital, the narrowest fiscal space, and the greatest barriers to accessing concessional resources. For SIDS, whose goal under the Antigua and Barbuda agenda is resilient prosperity, this contradiction is particularly acute. Our small economies, geographic remoteness, narrow productive bases, and exposure to external shocks and climate-related disasters make development more costly and recovery more difficult. At the same time, it should not be viewed only through the lens of vulnerability. We invest CAR's resources in protecting oceans, ecosystems, and biodiversity that provide global benefits. Therefore, financing seeds is an investment in global public goods, and denying affordable capital only compounds in global risk. First, vulnerability must matter in determining access to finance. GNI alone cannot tell us what a hurricane costs, what geographic isolation costs, or what repeated exposure to external shocks costs. Measures that complement and go beyond GDP, including the multidimensional vulnerability index, must move from recognition to meaningful use across the United Nations system, international financial institutions, and development partners. Second, we must confront the debt crisis as a development crisis. For too many states, scarce public resources that should finance hospitals, schools, resilient infrastructure, and economic transformation are instead absorbed by debt service. Development finance cannot mean indebting the vulnerable simply to withstand the next shock. The Seville commitment provides important avenues forward, and these commitments must now be operationalized. In particular, we call for urgent support to the SIDS Center of Excellence to fully operationalize the Debt Sustainability Support Service and translate this commitment into practical support. AOSIS also continues to support an ambitious intergovernmental process on debt and solutions that are timely, predictable, and responsive to the circumstances of our vulnerable countries. Third, declining public finance cannot simply be replaced by expensive private capital. We recognize the indispensable role of the private sector, but mobilizing private finance must mean directing investment towards sustainable development and not merely towards markets where returns are easiest and risk are lowest. Therefore, ODA remains indispensable, particularly for countries and sectors where private capital cannot or will not go. We therefore call on development partners to reverse these declines and fulfill their commitments. We also need greater use of guarantees, blended finance, and other instruments capable of reducing the cost of capital and unlocking investment in SIDS. Madam Chair, at a time when we aim to close financing gaps and accelerate achievement of the sustainable development goals, we should be removing barriers to development, not creating new ones. In this regard, AOSIS calls on states to refrain from unilateral coercive measures inconsistent with UN Charter and international law. In 2026, more than 118,600 lots were regularized, and that increased legal security in the protection of the families involved. Thank you.
I would like to invite for his statement the Permanent Representative of Armenia. Ambassador, you have the floor.

Thank you, Madam Chair. I congratulate you and members of Bureau on your election and wish you every success in guiding us. As we approach 2030, we must translate our commitments into concrete results through accessible financing, stronger national capacities, resilience infrastructure, technology, and effective partnerships. Armenia supports implementing the Sevilla commitment, including expanded access to affordable long-term financing, stronger support from multilateral development banks, and financing approaches that better reflect countries' multidimensional vulnerabilities. These priorities are reflected in the Armenia UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework for 2026-2030. Aligned with our national priorities, it advances human capital and well-being, inclusive economic development, green transition, and governance. National ownership, capacity development, and resource mobilization are central to its implementation. Madam Chair, financing sustainable development must also address the environmental dimension of 2030 agenda. As host and incoming presidency of COP 17 on biodiversity, Armenia is committed to an inclusive, transparent and action-oriented conference that advances implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. COP 17 will undertake the first global review of collective progress under the framework, assessing achievements and gaps and identifying where accelerated action is needed. We will prioritize mobilizing adequate, predictable and accessible biodiversity finance and strengthening implementation of the multilateral benefit sharing mechanism for digital sequence information on genetic resources, including the Gali Fund. We will also promote synergies among biodiversity, conservation, climate action, and efforts to combat land degradation while addressing pollution. Meaningful participation, monitoring, and accountability will be essential to translate the commitments into measurable results. Madam Chair, as both a landlocked and middle-income country, Armenia emphasizes that income levels alone cannot capture a country's development needs and structural vulnerabilities. We support developing a strategic plan of action for middle-income countries, anchored in national priorities and ownership. It should strengthen coordinated UN support and access to financing, technology, and capacity building without duplicating frameworks or creating additional reporting burdens. We also emphasize the full and effective implementation of the AVASA Programme of Action for landlocked developing countries to address infrastructure gaps, reduce trade costs, and strengthen resilience to supply chain disruptions. Armenia continues to advance the Crossroad of Peace initiative, including its integral component, the Trip Connectivity Project, on the basis of sovereignty, territorial integrity, national jurisdiction, and reciprocity. It aims to strengthen trade and transport links to the South Caucasus and expand the region's integration into international routes and global supply chains. In conclusion, Armenia remains ready to work with all partners to advance the 2030 Agenda, and we look forward to welcoming you to Yerevan for COP17. I thank you.
Thank you, Ambassador, for your statement. Now, I would like to invite the Permanent Representative of the Lao People's Democratic Republic to take the floor. Ambassador, you have the floor.

Thank you, Madam Chair. At the outset, I congratulate you, Madam Chair, and the Bureau on your election to the Second Committee. We assure you of our full support and cooperation. My delegation aligns itself with the statements delivered on behalf of the groups of 77 and China, ASEAN, and NDCs, and adds the following remarks in our national capacity. As we enter the critical final period of the 2030 agenda, the global development landscape remains challenging. Geopolitical tensions, economic fragmentations, Rising debt burdens and declining development assistance are constraining developing countries' capacity to invest in sustainable development. The approximately $4 trillion annual SDG financing gap underscores the urgency of translating commitments into concrete resources and actions. Against this backdrop, We underscore the importance of renewed political commitment to multilateralism and international cooperation, particularly with the Seville commitment. Its implementation should place the needs of developing countries, particularly the Global South, at the center. In this connection, we are pleased that development remains a core of the United Nations system. We support efforts to reposition the UN development system and the UN80 initiative that aim at improving efficiency and effectiveness while safeguarding the UN's development mandate and supporting countries most in need. Also, we must strengthen the availability and quality of development resources amid declining ODA, shrinking fiscal space, and mounting debt servicing pressure for developing countries. We therefore call for stronger resource mobilization, increased grants and concessional support, and the fulfilment of long-standing ODA commitments, including the 0.7% of GNI target. Importantly, stronger attention should be given to the group of countries in special situations who require adequate and tailored support. This includes areas of climate finance, technology transfer, capacity building, and enhanced market access. Madam Chair, for the Lao PDR, our graduation from the LDC category in November this year, we marked an important development milestone. By implementing our smooth transition strategy, we aim to advance macroeconomic stability, economic diversification, structural transformation, and climate and disaster resilience. We will continue strengthening domestic resources mobilization and attracting sustainable investment while requiring continued international support measures to safeguard development gains and ensure a sustainable and irreversible transition. We also attach great importance to connectivity and structural transformation. Through regional integration, trade facilitation, and infrastructure development, We are advancing our vision of transforming from a landlocked to a land-linked country. We, in this regard, encourage strengthened implementation of LDCs, our program of action, and its developments. Climate action must remain integral to sustainable development. Despite our limited contribution to global emissions, the Lao PDR remains highly vulnerable to climate change and natural disasters. the call for predictable and accessible climate resources, particularly for developing countries with limited fiscal space. Furthermore, we recognize the growing potential of artificial intelligence to accelerate sustainable development. At the same time, inclusive, transparent, and development-oriented AI governance is essential to ensure equitable access to its benefits address emerging risks and prevent new forms of digital inequality, particularly for developing countries. To conclude, Madam Chair, the challenge before us is not a lack of commitment, but ensuring implementation. The Lao PDR stands ready to work constructively with our partners and the UN system to accelerate SDG implementation in this fast-changing global environment. I thank you, Madam Chair.
Thank you, Ambassador, for your statement. Now I would like to invite for his statement the Permanent Representative of State of Palestine. Ambassador, you have the floor.

Madam Chair, the State of Palestine aligns itself with the statement delivered by Uruguay on behalf of the Group of 77 and join other delegations in congratulating you and other members of the Bureau on your election to lead the Second Committee. You can count on Palestine's full support to ensure the success of the main session of the Second Committee. Madam Chair, Excellencies, it is clear with four years left to 2030, the implementation of the SDGs is facing alarming setbacks. From deepening inequalities to persistent injustices, the gap between our promises and the realities faced by hundreds of millions of people is growing wider. While technology and innovation have reached unprecedented levels, hunger and poverty remain at unacceptable levels. While military spending rises, development financing remains far below what is needed to achieve the SDGs. While some countries have advanced, too many are being left behind. These global setbacks are not headlines or trends. They are daily realities, and the people of Palestine know this reality all too well. For Palestine, this reality is not only compounded by the same challenges faced by fellow developing countries, but are compounded by a ruthless settler colonial occupation that has unleashed a genocide against our people. One that Secretary-General Antonio Guterres described during the general debate of the General Assembly, an onslaught with a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all of my years as Secretary-General. This has devastated every dimension of sustainable development and undermined its very foundations in Palestine. First, the social dimension of sustainable development. The ongoing Israeli genocide has not only destroyed lives, torn families apart, and denied futures, but has also stolen generations of immeasurable human potential. It killed over 75,000 of our people in less than three years, including 22,000 children. It killed more than 38,000 women and girls, with 47 Palestinian women and girls killed by Israel every day for over two years. It weaponized hunger and unleashed a manmade famine that drove food insecurity to catastrophic levels that should not exist in the 21st century. Second, the economic dimension of sustainable development. It inflicted the fastest and most devastating economic collapse ever recorded by erasing 22 years of Palestine's economic progress in just 15 months and erasing 77 years of human development in Gaza. Third, the developmental dimension of sustainable development. It destroyed more than 371,000 homes and unleashed 68 million metric tons of hazardous debris, equivalent in volume to 15 Great Pyramids of Giza or 25,000 Eiffel Towers. Madam Chair, the 2030 agenda emphasizes that there can be no sustainable development without peace and no peace without sustainable development. The SDGs cannot flourish without justice. They cannot be implemented where accountability is absent, and they cannot be achieved where international law is selectively applied. This requires ending the Israeli colonial occupation, ensuring justice and accountability, and restoring the conditions necessary for sustainable development. Let us, therefore, renew our commitment to international cooperation, to multilateralism, and to the principles of the UN Charter and international law by ensuring that our collective efforts are measured not only by the commitments we make, but by the lives we seek to improve, and above all, by the countries and people we refuse to leave behind. I thank you.
Thank you, Ambassador, for your statement. Now I would like to invite the Permanent Representative of Malaysia to deliver her statement. Ambassador, you have the floor.

I would like to first congratulate you and the other members of the Bureau on your election. Malaysia assures you of our full support throughout this session. Malaysia aligns itself with the statement delivered by Uruguay on behalf of G77 and China, and by the Philippines on behalf of ASEAN. Madam Chair, the theme of this year's general debate, financing sustainable development in a changing global economy to accelerate implementation of the SDG, remains immensely relevant to us. As we approach the final years of the 2030 agenda, the financing to deliver sustainable development remains under considerable strain. For many developing countries, progress towards the SDGs continues to be challenged by persistent financing gaps, climate pressures, and global economic uncertainties. Addressing these challenges requires continued international cooperation and a more responsive global financial system. Malaysia remains firmly committed to the implementation of the 2030 agenda. Our third Voluntary National Review in 2025 reaffirms our determination to pursue development that is inclusive, sustainable, and resilient. While Malaysia has made important progress across the SDGs, we recognize that further efforts are required to translate our ambitions into tangible improvements in the livelihoods of our people. Financing must remain at the heart of these efforts. Developing countries require not only accessible financing, but it must also be paired with adequate capacity building. This should be supported by an equitable international financial architecture that responds to development priorities. Malaysia believes that financing alone will not be sufficient. We must strengthen the means of implementation through innovation and South-South and triangular cooperation. Partnerships must translate global commitments into practical solutions that leave no one behind. Madam Chair, climate change remains inseparable from our development efforts. Malaysia remains committed to pursuing a just and inclusive transition towards a low-carbon, climate-resilient economy. To achieve this, ambitious climate action must go hand in hand with the necessary support and safeguards. As an incoming member of ECOSOC for the term 2027-2029, Malaysia looks forward to contributing constructively in accelerating the implementation of the 2030 agenda. We will continue to advocate for a multilateral system that places sustainable development at its core. The Second Committee has an important responsibility in advancing this collective endeavor. Malaysia stands ready to work with all Member States to strengthen development cooperation, advance international financial architecture reform, and accelerate progress towards the SDGs. The remaining years to 2030 demand greater and collective action. Our primary task is to ensure that commitments made at the UN are matched by the implementation necessary to deliver meaningful results on the ground. Thank you.
Thank you, Ambassador, for your statement. Now I would like to invite the distinguished delegate of India to take the floor. You have the floor, India.

I congratulate you and the Bureau on your election and thank you for choosing a very relevant topic for today's general debate. India associates itself with the statement delivered by the Group of 77 and China. The outlook for many developing countries remains deeply concerning. Official development assistance fell sharply in 2025. Disruptions to food, fuel, and fertilizer supplies raise costs far beyond the places where fighting occurs. For countries with limited fiscal space, a higher import bill can mean less investment in their people. For many, the immediate challenge is not only to accelerate progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals, but to protect hard-won gains. These pressures expose a deeply imbalance. Developing countries bear much of the cost of global instability, yet remains inadequately represented in the international financial institutions whose decisions shape their access to finance. They need a greater voice in those decisions alongside more affordable and predictable financing. Madam Chair, India approaches this debate with the experience of financing development for more than 1.4 billion people. We have strengthened domestic resources, mobilization, including through digitalization of tax administration. Our digital public infrastructure has expanded financial inclusion and access to services, while helping people and small businesses participate in the formal economy and obtain finance. We are also building a pipeline for public-private partnership projects and developing instruments to attract capital into infrastructure. Private investments has the greatest development impact when it serves nationally identified priorities and is supported by sound public institutions. We bring that conviction to our partnership with the Global South. The India UN Development Partnership Fund and the India, Brazil and South Africa Fund supports projects identified by the partner countries. The International Solar Alliance and the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure help translate cooperation on clean energy and resilience into action. Our BRICS chairship this year offered another opportunity to address the financing challenge. India and the New Development Bank have brought together governments and the private sector to examine how more capital can reach sustainable development projects. Madam Chair, ahead of the 2027 SDG Summit, discussion of development beyond 2030 must begin with an honest account of what has impeded delivery on our existing goals. India supports an agenda that carries forward the SDGs unfinished work and respects national ownership. UN80 reform must strengthen the development pillars ability to help member states turn that agenda into results. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of India. And now I'd like to give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mexico.

Muchas gracias.

Many thanks, Madam Chair. And congratulations on your appointment, and also the other members of the Bureau. And we wish you every success in your work. Mexico is participating in this general debate, convinced that restoring trust and confidence and managing change is essential for the United Nations. and to generation of concrete results for everybody. Almost three years from 2030, we are facing persistent inequalities and economic, social and environmental crises that are deeply interconnected. Given that situation, poverty eradication in all its forms and dimensions and the reduction of inequalities must remain at the center. Our experience confirms that fighting poverty is one of the main accelerators of sustainable development. Between 2018 and 2024, more than 13.4 million people have been lifted out of poverty in Mexico, and in 2026, our welfare programs reached 42.8 million people. Mexico remains convinced that multilateralism is the best tool for facing up to common challenges, but defending it also means making it more effective. We therefore welcome the recent revitalization of the working methods of the Second Commission. That's the only GA commission that has taken on an exercise of this type. Although the results don't quite reflect the level of ambition that Mexico would have liked, we welcome the readiness of the Group of 77 and China, and all delegations who made it possible to come to an agreement. This is of particular importance given the UN80 initiative, whose spirit we hope will prevail and be strengthened. In the case of mandates, we must avoid duplication, respect decisions of the members, and concentrate our efforts where we can really add value without reducing ambition or weakening substantive commitments. Development activities on the ground must consider that harmony with a system that is equipped and integrated to address the most urgent needs. Madam Chair, Mexico will uphold the integrity of the 2030 agenda and the SDGs. We are particularly concerned by reversals in the agreed language on gender equality, inequality reduction, inclusion and sustainable development. This is of particular importance given the SDG summit of 2027. The agreement built since 2015 must be strengthened rather than weakened. For Mexico, any vision of the future must have sustainable development as a holistic agenda based on poverty eradication, closing the financing gap and strengthening the United Nations development system by avoiding fragmentation. Mexico will continue to promote the implementation of the Cevier commitment and a more inclusive, representative and development-oriented international financial architecture. We must mobilize more and better resources, strengthen the role of development banks and make use of the private sector as an ally or partner to produce sustainable investment and decent jobs. Mexico will continue defending a progressive agenda in terms of agriculture, food safety, nutrition and the right to food, and also recognising migrants as agents of development. In the face of the triple planetary crisis, Mexico will promote a holistic vision that brings together climate action, biodiversity, water and the oceans, with responses based on science and international cooperation. We will continue to promote ambitious, just and inclusive climate action that strengthens adaptation and resilience, particularly among the most vulnerable communities, and that contributes to an energy transition that is just, orderly and equitable. Water must have a central place in that agenda. The upcoming United Nations Water Conference 2026 represents an opportunity to speed up the implementation of Goal 6, strengthen cooperation and improve the coherence of the multilateral system with regard to water. With regard to the oceans, Mexico will continue to promote the implementation of the agreement on marine biodiversity of areas beyond national jurisdiction, BBNJ, and better coordination in the areas of oceans, climate and biodiversity. Madam Chair, Mexico is coming to this session ready to build bridges, facilitate agreements and promote a better link between our work and what's happening on the ground. We will work with all of the members to protect what has been built, comply with what's been agreed and build new consensus with a view to 2030. And more than that, we will keep the centre. Thank you very much.
Now I give the floor to the last speaker for today's morning session, distinguished representative of Philippines, you have the floor.

Thank you so much, Madam Chair, and at the outset, we wish to congratulate you and your members on your election. Rest assured of our delegation's support and constructive engagement in the work of the Second Committee. The Philippines aligned itself with the statement delivered by Uruguay on behalf of the G77 and China, and that of ASEAN. With only a few years before 2030, accelerating action to realize the SDGs should remain our collective objective. In this context, the Philippines highlights the following priorities for this session. First, enhancing support for middle-income countries. We welcome the progress to elaborate a strategic plan of action for MICs, mandated by GA Resolution 80/149, and the Secretary-General's consultations with member states, UN agencies, and other stakeholders. As chair of the like-minded group for middle income countries, the Philippines will continue to promote a strategic plan of action that fosters a new development paradigm and addresses the middle income trap. Second, financing for development and development cooperation. Earlier this year, the Philippines attained upper middle income country status. However, income classification alone cannot fully capture the realities, circumstances, and structural vulnerabilities faced by middle income countries. Hence, the beyond GDP process must remain a priority. In line with severe commitment, the Philippines urges stronger international cooperation to mobilize development financing, facilitate technology transfer and capacity building, as well as reform of the international financial architecture. Third, agriculture and food security. Conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have disrupted global maritime trade and supply chains. contributing to food insecurity and economic shocks for many countries. The impacts of climate change, including the anticipated El Nino, necessitate focused action. The Philippines supports efforts to enhance food security and agricultural productivity, including through enhanced trade facilitation and institutional reforms, which are essential components of poverty eradication and attainment of the SDGs. Fourth, climate action and disaster resilience. The recent landslide and floods in Nepal have given us a stark reminder that countries that have contributed the least to global emissions are bearing the brunt of climate change. As the host country of the Board for responding to loss and damage, the Philippines is committed to advancing climate resilient development and strengthening international cooperation to support the most vulnerable, including in disaster risk reduction. Fifth, migration for development. The positive contribution of migrants to sustainable development in countries of origin, transit, and destination must continue to be recognized. We call for stronger partnerships and global cooperation to leverage diasporas and address barriers to migrants' meaningful participation in mobilizing private finance, including in lowering the cost of remittances, as called for in the Cevier commitment. Sixth, digital transformation and artificial intelligence. Recognizing the potential of AI to support developing countries, we highlight the urgent need for AI governance that harnesses AI responsibly, enhances productivity, improves public service, bridges digital divides, and protects human dignity. Seventh, South-South and triangular cooperation. South-South and triangular cooperation can help mobilize expertise, resources, and technologies to support national development priorities. The Philippines supports mainstreaming South-South and triangular cooperation as a catalyst for sustainable development. In conclusion, Madam Chair, at the general debate of High-Level Week this year, the Philippines underscored the need to always put a face to what we do, as our work here should ultimately bring about real life and positive impact in our communities and on our peoples. Let us seize this opportunity and demonstrate that multilateralism and indeed deliver for people, planet, and prosperity. I thank you, Madam Chair.

I thank the distinguished representative of Philippines. And with this statement, we have concluded the morning session. Before adjourning the meeting, I would like to recall you that we'll meet at 3 o'clock in the same room for the continuation of the general debate. The meeting is adjourned.
